entries.h: 🔥 Reduce or Neutralize Acid & Protect the Ulcer
entries.t: Omeprazole / Pantoprazole PPI Use: GERD, PUD, gastritis, H. pylori, stress-ulcer prevention. Key points: Blocks the gastric proton pump — the final step of acid production. Take 30–60 min before meals; don't crush delayed-release forms. Wat

entries.h: 🔄 Move the Gut & Stop Nausea (Motility & Antiemetics)
entries.t: Metoclopramide (Reglan) PROKINETIC / ANTIEMETIC Use: Gastroparesis, GERD, nausea, dumping-related symptoms. Key points: Speeds gastric emptying and raises LES tone. Give before meals and at bedtime. Watch: Extrapyramidal symptoms / tardive

Loperamide (Imodium) ANTIDIARRHEAL Use: Acute and chronic diarrhea (non-infectious). Key points: Slows intestinal motility so more water is reabsorbed. Not for the child or the patient with bloody stool/fever. Watch: Avoid in C. diff or inf

Psyllium (Metamucil) BULK-FORMING LAXATIVE Use: Constipation; safest for long-term/daily use; also IBS. Key points: Absorbs water to add soft bulk and stimulate peristalsis. Take with a full glass of water. Watch: Too little fluid can cause

Mesalamine / Sulfasalazine AMINOSALICYLATE (5-ASA) Use: IBD — maintain remission in UC & Crohn. Key points: Anti-inflammatory action on the bowel mucosa. Maintenance drug (not for acute rescue). Watch: Sulfasalazine: give with food + fluids

Metronidazole (Flagyl) ANTIBIOTIC Use: Diverticulitis, intra-abdominal infection, C. difficile. Key points: Anti-anaerobic/antiprotozoal. Complete the full course. Watch: No alcohol during and 3 days after — disulfiram-like reaction; metall

Cyanocobalamin (Vitamin B12) VITAMIN SUPPLEMENT Use: Pernicious anemia; post-gastrectomy. Key points: Replaces B12 that can't be absorbed without intrinsic factor. Given as lifelong IM injections. Watch: Oral B12 won't work without intrinsi

entries.h: 🚨 The traps that cost you the most points

entries.t: The single most common miss. If the stem ends in indicates, suggests, or the nurse interprets, the answer is a name for the problem, not a thing you do.

entries.h: Picking the intervention you would do second
entries.t: On a "first" question, several options are things you genuinely would do. Assess before you intervene — unless the client is unstable, in which case act first. Never pick "notify the provider" if there is something you must assess or do in

On "which client first," the sick-looking-but-expected client is bait. A day-two temperature of 100.2 F is expected. A new, unexpected, or worsening finding wins — especially airway, breathing, or circulation.
"Which statement indicates the client needs FURTHER teaching" means you are hunting for the wrong statement. Read the last six words of every stem twice.
On "generate solutions," anything starting with "The nurse will…" is almost always wrong. A goal describes what the client will do, by when.

The formula only works when Desired and Have are in the same unit. If the order says grams and the bottle says milligrams, fix that first. This is where most wrong answers come from. Order: 0.5 g. Label: 250 mg tablets. Step 1 — same units:
Half a tablet, 2 tablets, 5–15 mL of a liquid: reasonable. 38 tablets or 0.006 mL: you slipped a decimal. On a test, an answer that is off by exactly 1000 almost always means a mg/mcg mix-up.

entries.h: 🍎 Nutrition (Modules 9 & 10) Diet therapy for Renal/Urinary & Hepatobiliary disorders · ATI Nutrition Ch. 14–
entries.t: Big picture: Two dials dominate this exam's nutrition — protein (the renal "flip") and fat (the hepatobiliary lever). Nail those two and most questions fall into place. 🫘 Renal & Urinary Nutrition (Module 9) Urea is the waste product of pr
Diet therapy for Renal/Urinary & Hepatobiliary disorders · ATI Nutrition Ch. 14–15
Urea is the waste product of protein metabolism. It rises as kidneys fail, so protein is the master dial — but which way you turn it depends on dialysis.

RESTRICT protein 0.8–1.0 g/kg/day, high biologic value (eggs, meat, fish, soy, dairy). Restrict sodium (for BP) and potassium (prevent hyperkalemia). Restrict phosphorus — limit peanut butter, beans, bran, cola, chocolate, beer to ≤1 servin

On dialysis, protein INCREASES to 1.0–1.2 g/kg (amino acids are lost in the dialysate). Still low sodium (2–3 g), low potassium, low phosphorus (700–1,200 mg), fluid-restricted, ~35 kcal/kg, phosphate binders with meals.
Usually reversible. 20–30 cal/kg. Protein 0.6 g/kg (no dialysis) → 1.0–1.2 (on dialysis). Fluid = urine output + 500 mL when oliguric.
Proteinuria + edema. Adequate protein 0.7–1.0 g/kg (soy helps), LOW sodium (2,000 mg), carbs for calories, low cholesterol/fat, vitamins.
Mostly calcium oxalate. #1 = FLUIDS for ≥2 L urine/day (including before bed). Limit animal protein, sodium, and oxalates (spinach, rhubarb, beets, nuts, chocolate, tea). No megadose vitamin C.

↑ Protein (positive nitrogen balance) · carbs NOT restricted · vitamins B, C, K · eliminate alcohol, nicotine, caffeine. (In hepatic encephalopathy, protein is temporarily moderated — but the default liver-diet answer is higher protein.)
LIMIT fat — dietary fat stimulates the inflamed gallbladder. Low-fat is the whole answer.
Acute: NPO + NG suction, TPN to rest the pancreas. Chronic: low-fat, high-protein, high-carb + vitamins C & B.

Condition Diet answer Low- vs high-fiber Low-fiber RESTS the gut (diarrhea, flares); high-fiber MOVES it (constipation, prevention). Constipation Fiber 25 g/day female · 38 g/day male; fluids 64 oz/day; exercise. Avoid chronic laxatives. Di

Liver protein released with inflammation anywhere. Nonspecific — says "something's inflamed," not what or where. Fast: rises 4–6 hrs, peaks ~48 hrs. That speed is why it's useful in acute infection. Trend it to see if antibiotics are workin
ESRD patients run a mildly elevated CRP (~5–10) from chronic inflammation. Hers is 61.5. That's acute infection, not noise.

"Highest risk" = what kills her fastest. On the NCLEX that's almost always sepsis.

Answer: B Early morning, empty stomach, 8 oz of water, and upright 30 minutes — that is what prevents esophagitis and esophageal ulcers. Calcium and food block absorption.

entries.h: An 82-year-old is admitted with new-onset confusion and agitation. What should the nurse assess FIRST?
entries.t: a. Reorient and keep monitoring b. Assume it's early dementia c. Check for infection (UTI), hypoxia, and new medications d. Apply restraints for safety Check c. Sudden confusion = delirium until proven otherwise — hunt for a reversible caus

entries.h: A home-care nurse suspects an older client is being neglected by a caregiver. The nurse's responsibility is to
entries.t: a. Confront and warn the caregiver b. Wait for proof before acting c. Report the suspicion — nurses are mandatory reporters d. Do nothing unless the client asks Check c. Nurses are mandatory reporters — report suspicion (you don't need proo

entries.h: A client with CKD has a potassium of 6.8 mEq/L. Which finding is the priority concern?
entries.t: a. Peaked T waves on ECG b. Mild muscle cramps c. Nausea d. Warm skin Check a. Hyperkalemia → peaked T waves → wide QRS → arrest. Cardiac effects are the priority; anticipate calcium gluconate, insulin + D50.

entries.h: An order reads "potassium chloride 20 mEq IV push." The nurse should:
entries.t: a. Give slowly over 2 minutes b. Never give KCl IV push — hold and clarify c. Give with a saline flush d. Dilute in 10 mL and push Check b. IV KCl is NEVER pushed (fatal dysrhythmia) — always diluted on a pump, max ~10 mEq/hr; confirm urine

entries.h: ABG: pH 7.30, PaCO₂ 38, HCO₃ 16. This represents:
entries.t: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Metabolic acidosis c. Respiratory alkalosis d. Metabolic alkalosis Check b. Low pH + low HCO₃ (metabolic value moves the same direction as pH) = metabolic acidosis — think DKA, diarrhea, renal failure. CO₂ is norm

entries.h: A post-op client's abdominal incision opens and loops of bowel protrude. The nurse's first action?
entries.t: a. Push the organs back in b. Cover with sterile saline-soaked gauze, low-Fowler knees bent, call surgeon c. Apply a dry pressure dressing d. Give oral fluids Check b. Evisceration: cover with sterile saline-moistened gauze, low-Fowler with

entries.h: Which statement about acetaminophen needs correction?
entries.t: a. "I won't exceed 4 grams a day" b. "I'll check cold medicines for acetaminophen too" c. "It's fine to have several drinks with it daily" d. "Overdose can damage my liver" Check c. Alcohol + acetaminophen ↑ hepatotoxicity; combo products s

entries.h: A nurse notes continuous bubbling in the water-seal chamber of a chest drainage system. This indicates:
entries.t: a. Normal function b. An air leak — check connections and the insertion site c. The lung has fully re-expanded d. Suction is too low Check b. Tidaling (rise/fall with breathing) is normal; continuous bubbling in the water seal = air leak. G

entries.h: What is the appropriate oxygen goal for a client with COPD?
entries.t: a. SpO₂ 88–92% b. SpO₂ exactly 100% c. 15 L non-rebreather routinely d. Withhold oxygen entirely Check a. Low-flow O₂ titrated to 88–92%. Excessive O₂ can blunt the hypoxic drive in chronic CO₂ retainers — but never withhold needed oxygen.

entries.h: During an asthma attack the wheezing suddenly stops and the chest is silent. This means:
entries.t: a. The attack is resolving b. The medication worked c. Airflow is severely obstructed — an emergency d. The client is relaxed Check c. A silent chest = no air movement = impending respiratory failure. Escalate immediately.

entries.h: Before giving digoxin, the apical pulse is 54 and regular. The nurse should:
entries.t: a. Give the dose b. Hold the dose and notify the provider c. Give half the dose d. Recheck in 4 hours after giving Check b. Hold digoxin if apical HR <60. Also watch toxicity (yellow-green halos, N/V) — and hypokalemia raises toxicity risk.

entries.h: Which rhythm is treated with defibrillation?
entries.t: a. Asystole b. Pulseless electrical activity c. Ventricular fibrillation d. Sinus bradycardia Check c. Shockable = V-fib and pulseless V-tach. Asystole/PEA get CPR + epinephrine, not a shock.

entries.h: Which finding should a client with heart failure report to the provider?
entries.t: a. Weight gain of 3 lb in one day b. Occasional mild fatigue c. Urinating in the morning d. Losing 1 lb over two weeks Check a. Rapid gain (2–3 lb/day or 5 lb/week) signals fluid retention/worsening HF. Daily weights, same scale/time.

entries.h: A client has a new AV fistula in the left arm for hemodialysis. Which action is correct?
entries.t: a. Take BPs in the left arm b. Draw labs from the fistula c. Assess for thrill/bruit; use the right arm for BP and sticks d. Keep the arm tightly wrapped Check c. Feel the thrill, hear the bruit each shift. No BP, IV, or venipuncture in the

entries.h: A client on peritoneal dialysis has cloudy outflow (effluent). This suggests:
entries.t: a. Normal dialysate b. Peritonitis c. Too much fluid removed d. A kinked catheter Check b. Cloudy effluent = peritonitis, the major PD complication → notify, obtain culture, sterile technique.

entries.h: Lactulose is prescribed for hepatic encephalopathy. The nurse titrates to achieve:
entries.t: a. 2–3 soft stools per day b. No bowel movements c. Firm formed stools d. 8–10 watery stools per day Check a. Lactulose traps and excretes ammonia in stool; goal is 2–3 soft stools/day (too many → dehydration).

entries.h: After a laparoscopic cholecystectomy a client reports right shoulder pain. The nurse recognizes this as:
entries.t: a. A sign of hemorrhage b. Expected referred pain from CO₂ gas — encourage ambulation c. A myocardial infarction d. Bile duct injury Check b. Insufflated CO₂ irritates the diaphragm → referred shoulder pain. Normal — ambulation and position

entries.h: After an EGD with moderate sedation, which must the nurse assess before offering fluids?
entries.t: a. Bowel sounds b. Return of the gag reflex c. Orientation ×3 d. Ability to ambulate Check b. The throat is anesthetized — anything PO before the gag reflex returns risks aspiration. Airway first.

entries.h: Teaching for dumping syndrome — select all correct:
entries.t: a. Drink fluids with meals b. Small, frequent meals c. High-protein, higher-fat foods d. Lie down after eating e. Add sugar for energy Check b, c, d. Fluids with meals (a) and simple sugars (e) both worsen dumping. Drink 30–60 min before/af

entries.h: A duodenal ulcer client's pain suddenly stops; abdomen is rigid, HR 118, BP 96/60. First action?
entries.t: a. Document and monitor b. Give the scheduled PPI c. NPO and notify provider immediately d. Offer clear liquids Check c. Sudden pain relief + rigid abdomen + shock vitals = perforation with peritonitis. NPO, notify, prep for surgery.

entries.h: Acute diverticulitis — which orders would the nurse question? Select all:
entries.t: a. Clear liquid diet b. High-fiber diet now c. Colonoscopy today d. IV antibiotics e. Soap suds enema Check b, c, e. During a flare the bowel must rest — high fiber, scopes, and enemas raise perforation risk. High fiber is for AFTER healing

entries.h: TPN bag runs dry; next bag is an hour away. What should the nurse hang?
entries.t: a. 0.9% NS b. D10W c. Lactated Ringer's d. Keep line clamped Check b. Stopping TPN abruptly → rebound hypoglycemia. D10W at the same rate maintains glucose until the new bag arrives.

entries.h: Four ostomy clients call. Who does the nurse call back FIRST?
entries.t: a. New ileostomy: stoma bled slightly with cleaning b. Colostomy: no output for 3 hours c. Ileostomy: stoma looks dark purple d. New colostomy: stoma slightly swollen Check c. Dusky/purple stoma = ischemia = surgical emergency. The others a

entries.h: Which findings indicate Crohn (not UC)? Select all:
entries.t: a. Skip lesions, cobblestone b. Continuous inflammation from rectum c. Fistula formation d. 10–20 bloody stools/day e. B12 deficiency (terminal ileum) Check a, c, e = Crohn. Continuous rectal inflammation (b) and frequent bloody stools (d)

entries.h: Suspected peritonitis: BP 88/54, HR 126, rigid abdomen. First action?
entries.t: a. Insert NG tube b. Start IV fluid bolus as ordered c. Give IV antibiotic d. Position semi-Fowler Check b. These vitals = hypovolemia/early septic shock from third-spacing — restore circulation first. The rest follow quickly.

entries.h: Appendicitis client asks for a heating pad. The nurse declines because heat can:
entries.t: a. Mask symptoms b. Increase inflammation and cause rupture c. Interfere with skin prep d. Be less effective than cold Check b. Heat ↑ blood flow/inflammation → rupture → peritonitis. Same reason enemas and laxatives are banned.

entries.h: Which statement shows effective celiac teaching?
entries.t: a. "Whole-grain wheat bread is fine" b. "I'll avoid gluten only until my gut heals" c. "Rice, corn, and potatoes are safe" d. "A little beer on weekends is okay" Check c. Gluten-free is lifelong and strict. Wheat (a), any time limit (b), an

entries.h: SBO with NG tube to suction — anticipated lab finding?
entries.t: a. Metabolic acidosis + hyperkalemia b. Metabolic alkalosis + hypokalemia c. Respiratory alkalosis d. No change Check b. Losing gastric HCl + K⁺ through suction/vomiting → metabolic alkalosis + hypokalemia.

entries.h: A client on sulfasalazine for UC needs more teaching when they say:
entries.t: a. "Orange urine is expected" b. "Take with food and water" c. "I'll take folic acid" d. "I'll stop it when my diarrhea stops" Check d. 5-ASAs are maintenance — stopping when symptoms resolve invites relapse.

entries.h: hours after casting a tibial fracture, the client reports deep pain unrelieved by opioids and worse when toes
entries.t: a. Elevate the leg above the heart and apply ice b. Give another opioid dose and reassess in 1 hr c. Notify the provider immediately — suspect compartment syndrome d. Reassure that pain is normal after casting Check c. Pain out of proportio

entries.h: hours after a long-bone fracture, a client has confusion, SpO₂ 88%, and a petechial rash on the chest. Which
entries.t: a. Administer oxygen b. Start a heparin drip c. Notify the provider d. Prepare for possible BiPAP/intubation e. Maintain bed rest Check a, c, d, e. Classic fat embolism triad — treatment is supportive (O₂, respiratory support, rest). Hepari

entries.h: Which statement by a post-op total hip (posterior) client needs correction?
entries.t: a. "I'll keep a pillow between my legs" b. "I'll use a raised toilet seat" c. "I can bend forward to tie my shoes" d. "I won't cross my legs" Check c. Bending forward flexes the hip >90° → dislocation risk. Abduction pillow, raised seat, an

entries.h: Pantoprazole 40 mg in 100 mL NS over 30 min. Pump rate?
entries.t: a. 100 mL/hr b. 150 mL/hr c. 200 mL/hr d. 300 mL/hr Check c. 100 mL ÷ 30 min × 60 = 200 mL/hr.

entries.h: Infliximab 5 mg/kg IV for a client weighing 176 lb. Dose?
entries.t: a. 320 mg b. 400 mg c. 440 mg d. 880 mg Check b. 176 ÷ 2.2 = 80 kg × 5 mg = 400 mg.

entries.h: ,000 mL LR over 8 hr, drop factor 15 gtt/mL. Drip rate?
entries.t: a. 21 gtt/min b. 25 gtt/min c. 31 gtt/min d. 42 gtt/min Check c. 125 mL/hr × 15 ÷ 60 = 31.25 → 31 gtt/min.

entries.h: Metronidazole 500 mg PO TID, available 250 mg tabs. Tablets per DAY?
entries.t: a. 2 b. 3 c. 4 d. 6 Check d. 2 tabs/dose × 3 doses = 6 tabs/day. Watch per-dose vs per-day.

entries.h: Heparin 25,000 units in 250 mL D5W, ordered at 800 units/hr. Pump rate (mL/hr)?
entries.t: a. 6 mL/hr b. 8 mL/hr c. 10 mL/hr d. 12 mL/hr Check b. Concentration = 25,000 units ÷ 250 mL = 100 units/mL. 800 ÷ 100 = 8 mL/hr.

🛡️ acetylcysteine Give within 8–10 hr for best effect. Watch the rising AST/ALT, not the symptoms — the client can look fine while the liver is failing.
🛡️ naloxone Shorter half-life than most opioids — it can wear off and the client re-sedates. Keep monitoring.
🛡️ flumazenil Can trigger seizures in chronic users or mixed TCA overdose. Use cautiously.
🛡️ vitamin K (phytonadione) Add FFP or PCC when bleeding is active — vitamin K alone is too slow.
🛡️ protamine sulfate 1 mg protamine per ~100 units heparin. Monitor aPTT.
🛡️ protamine sulfate (partial) Only reverses about 60% — LMWH is not fully reversible.
🛡️ idarucizumab (Praxbind) Direct thrombin inhibitor with its own dedicated antidote.
🛡️ andexanet alfa Factor Xa inhibitors. Expensive, not stocked everywhere.
🛡️ digoxin immune Fab (DigiFab) Anorexia, nausea, yellow-green halos. Hypokalemia worsens toxicity.
🛡️ calcium gluconate Classic in OB. First sign is loss of deep tendon reflexes, then respiratory depression.
🛡️ deferoxamine Urine turns a reddish 'vin rosé' color as iron is chelated out.
🛡️ succimer, edetate calcium disodium Chelation. Find the exposure source before discharge.
🛡️ atropine + pralidoxime SLUDGE — salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, GI upset, emesis.
🛡️ hydroxocobalamin Suspect after enclosed-space smoke inhalation. Turns urine and skin red.
🛡️ 100% oxygen (hyperbaric if severe) Pulse ox reads falsely normal — draw a carboxyhemoglobin level.
🛡️ leucovorin (folinic acid) 'Leucovorin rescue.' Hydrate and alkalinize the urine.
🛡️ fomepizole (or ethanol) Blocks alcohol dehydrogenase so the toxic metabolite never forms.
🛡️ glucagon Glucagon bypasses the blocked beta receptor. Atropine first for bradycardia.
🛡️ IV calcium + glucagon + high-dose insulin Verapamil and diltiazem drop both rate and pressure.
🛡️ sodium bicarbonate Watch for a widening QRS — that is the sign to treat, not the level.
🛡️ sugammadex, or neostigmine + glycopyrrolate Sugammadex encapsulates rocuronium and vecuronium.
🛡️ physostigmine 'Mad as a hatter, red as a beet, dry as a bone, hot as a hare, blind as a bat.'
🛡️ dextrose 50%, glucagon Conscious and able to swallow? 15 g fast carbs, recheck in 15 min.
🛡️ dantrolene Malignant hyperthermia. Earliest sign is rising end-tidal CO2, not fever.
🛡️ phentolamine Stop the infusion, leave the catheter in to aspirate, then infiltrate the site.
🛡️ aminocaproic acid Stop the infusion first. Have blood products ready.
🛡️ calcium gluconate first Calcium protects the heart, it does not lower the potassium.
🛡️ pyridoxine (vitamin B6) Also given routinely with INH to prevent peripheral neuropathy.
🛡️ calcium gluconate Tingling around the mouth, tremors, prolonged QT. See the Blood Products page.
🛡️ epinephrine Then antihistamines, steroids, oxygen and fluids.

entries.h: 🚨 The rules that apply to every transfusion
entries.t: Two RNs verify client ID, blood type and unit number at the bedside. Normal saline is the ONLY compatible fluid. Lactated Ringer's clots the line; dextrose lyses the cells. Stay with the client for the first 15 minutes and run slowly — that

entries.h: ⭐ Any reaction — the order of actions
entries.t: 1. STOP the transfusion → 2. NS with NEW tubing → 3. Vitals + assess → 4. Notify provider + blood bank → 5. Send bag, tubing & samples New tubing matters — if you keep the old line open you keep infusing the product.

entries.h: 🚨 Three rules that keep you out of trouble
entries.t: Only normal saline goes with blood. No LR in liver failure or hyperkalemia. It contains potassium and needs the liver to convert lactate. Correct sodium slowly — no more than about 8-10 mEq/L in 24 hours.

entries.h: ⭐ Empty stomach or with food? The one-line version
entries.t: Empty stomach = food would block absorption. With food = the drug would tear up the stomach, or food helps it absorb. Before meals = it has to be in place before the food arrives.
